🤖 AI NEWS ROUNDUP — October 2, 2026

1️⃣ TAVUS GRIFFIN PASSES THE VIDEO TURING TEST

Tavus unveiled Griffin, a live video-avatar model it calls the first Human Interaction Model. In real-time one-minute video calls, 48% of participants believed they had been talking to an actual human, compared with a pass rate under 3% for earlier systems. Griffin also ranks first on NVIDIA's benchmark for full-duplex AI video. Tavus presents it as a research preview, but the distance between "convincing avatar" and "indistinguishable from a person on a call" just collapsed.
🔹 @tavus

2️⃣ GOOGLE PUBLISHES THE PLAYBOOK BEHIND GEMINI'S FIVE NEW MATH PROOFS

A new Google paper, posted on arXiv, details Cogentic, a multi-agent system that produced original proofs for five previously unsolved problems. Instead of one long prompt, several agents explore different routes in parallel, dedicated checkers treat every step as false until proven, and verified results are stored for the next round. Most problems took only around 100 model calls, and human mathematicians confirmed each proof. The lesson for agent builders is blunt: a strict verifier plus a running record of proven work beats a cleverer prompt.
🔹 @rohanpaul_ai

3️⃣ OPENAI ULTRAFAST TAKES TOKEN SPEED TO 300 PER SECOND

OpenAI introduced Ultrafast, a premium speed tier that delivers up to 8x faster token generation, roughly 300 tokens per second in Codex and up to 6x in the API. It arrives first for GPT-6 Astra in Codex, ChatGPT Work and the API, with GPT-6.1 Sol to follow and a new Pro 500 plan offering the highest usage limits. In agentic coding loops, throughput is becoming the differentiator rather than raw intelligence.
🔹 @OpenAI

4️⃣ ANTHROPIC AND A HARVARD PHYSICIST NAME THE AI SCIENCE MISMATCH

Anthropic's Science Blog hosts Harvard physicist Matthew Schwartz on the impedance mismatch between frontier models and real research: two systems that each work well but fit together badly. His argument is that talking to a model the way you would talk to a human colleague is not the best way to draw out its scientific strength. Schwartz built a toolkit for exact quantitative calculations, and Claude surfaced connections to ecology, population genetics and a dozen other fields once domain experts steered it toward worthwhile questions.
🔹 @AnthropicAI

5️⃣ GITHUB HYDRAFUSION RUNS ONE TASK THROUGH MANY MODELS

GitHub shipped Project HydraFusion in the Copilot app and in VS Code. It is selected like any other model, but behind the scenes it routes a task across several models to draft, critique, revise or escalate, then returns a single answer. It is the clearest signal yet that everyday coding tools are moving from choosing a model to choosing a pipeline.
🔹 @github

6️⃣ NETFLIX PAID 587 MILLION FOR BEN AFFLECK'S FILM AI COMPANY

Ben Affleck described how InterPositive, the film AI company he co-founded in 2022, ended up acquired by Netflix in March for 587 million dollars in cash. His origin story is telling: after seeing early text to image work at OpenAI he briefly concluded film was finished and wanted to shoot as many movies as possible. The panic faded when he looked closer and found researchers brilliant at models but almost blank on how a shot is captured, lit and cut. That gap became the business.
🔹 @rohanpaul_ai

7️⃣ TENCENT MAKES AGENT SELF IMPROVEMENT CHEAPER AND STABLE

A new Tencent paper introduces SkillAdam, which rewrites an agent's instruction files without going in circles. Earlier auto-optimisation loops burn tokens because fresh edits quietly undo fixes that already worked. SkillAdam keeps a log of what has already been repaired and makes smaller changes when results are mixed. On long shopping and travel planning tasks it reached 28.3% average accuracy against 21.7% for the strongest earlier method, using about a third of the tokens.
🔹 @rohanpaul_ai

8️⃣ TERENCE TAO ON WHY TODAY'S MODELS STILL DO NOT FEEL INTELLIGENT

The mathematician Terence Tao put the unease many researchers feel into words: inspect how frontier systems solve problems and it does not feel like intelligence, more like cobbled together neural networks plus an algorithm that happened to work. After years of searching for an elusive intelligent way of thinking, he says it is simply not visible in the tools that actually solve the goals. A useful counterweight to launch week optimism.
🔹 @rohanpaul_ai

💭 The common thread this week is scaffolding, not raw capability. A video avatar that fools half of its testers, a proof engine that only works because its checkers assume every step is wrong, a coding feature that hides an entire model pipeline behind one menu entry, and an agent optimiser that wins by remembering its own past fixes all point the same way: the next gains come from how systems are organised, verified and measured, not from another jump in model size.

Which of these changes your daily workflow the most, the faster tokens, the multi-model pipelines, or the agent scaffolding tricks? 👇

Cloudflare Clef：Agent の「判断」専用 open-source model を Workers AI に投入

・本記事要約日: 2026-10-02
・本記事公開日: 2026-10-01

【この記事で1番言いたいことを一言で】

Cloudflare が、LLM に文章を生成させるのではなく、Agent が「次に何をすべきか」を数十〜数百msで判断するための decision model「Clef / Clef-flash」を Workers AI に投入した。

【3行-5行まとめ】

・Cloudflare Workers AI team が初めて自ら学習した open-source decision model「Clef」と「Clef-flash」を公開。
・自由な文章を生成するのではなく、入力状態と質問から、許可された各回答の probability を返す「判断」に特化した model。
・Clef は 27B、Clef-flash は 9B。どちらも 64K context window に対応し、最大64個の質問を1 request で処理できる。
・median latency は Clef が209.3ms、Clef-flashが38.8ms。Cloudflare の計測では Jev よりそれぞれ約2.5倍、約13倍高速。
・Workers AI から利用できるほか、model weights も Apache 2.0 license で公開された。

【本質の要約】

Clef は、ChatGPT のように文章を生成するための LLM ではない。

目的は、Agent や application の処理途中に入り、

「この問い合わせは緊急か？」
「どの team に送るべきか？」
「この操作を実行してよいか？」

といった構造化された判断を高速に返すことにある。

入力として state と typed question を渡すと、自由文ではなく、あらかじめ定義した回答候補ごとの probability を返す。

これにより、LLM の自由文を生成してから parse したり、reasoning の完了を待ったりせず、その結果をそのまま application logic に利用できる。

特に Agent の「hot path」、つまり request 処理中に毎回発生する高速な判断処理への組み込みを想定している。

【Clef と Clef-flash】

Clef
・Model: @cf/cloudflare/clef
・Size: 27B
・用途: 精度を優先する判断
・Context window: 64K tokens
・Median latency: 209.3ms
・p95: 238.6ms

Clef-flash
・Model: @cf/cloudflare/clef-flash
・Size: 9B
・用途: latency を重視する hot-path 判断
・Context window: 64K tokens
・Median latency: 38.8ms
・p95: 122.4ms

比較対象の Jev は Median 524.1ms、p95 536.0ms。

Cloudflare の計測では median で Clef は Jev の約2.5倍、Clef-flash は約13倍高速だった。

また、10種類の decision benchmark のうち、Clef 系 model が7つで最高 score を記録したとしている。

【3種類の判断方法】

Clef は System One API に対応し、1 request あたり最大64個の質問を処理できる。

noul
Yes / No の判断。Yes である probability を返す。

choice
あらかじめ指定した複数候補から選択。選択結果だけでなく、各候補の probability と confidence を返す。

score
定義した rubric に沿って評価。probability-weighted score と各 level の probability を返す。

つまり、

状態
↓
選択肢
↓
probability
↓
application が行動

という処理を作るための model になっている。

【想定されている用途】

Support triage
問い合わせの緊急度や担当 team を判断し、自動 route する。

Threat intelligence
Web site を category 分類する。Cloudflare の検証では Browser Run と組み合わせ、domain の取得・render・分類を2.2秒で実行した。同じ workflow の gpt-oss-120b は4.7秒だった。

Trust and safety
投稿内容などを独自 policy rubric に照らして score 化し、その probability に基づいて処理する。

Agent guardrails
Agent が tool を実行する直前に「この操作を実行してよいか」を数十ms程度で判断させる。

Visual classification
state と一緒に最大4枚の画像を渡せる。Clef は vision encoder を搭載している。

【何が新しいのか】

最大のポイントは、Cloudflare が Workers AI で他社 model を host するだけでなく、Cloudflare Workers AI team 自身が model を学習して公開したこと。

その最初の model が、汎用 LLM ではなく Agent の decision に特化した Clef / Clef-flash となった。

さらに、

・Workers AI 上で serverless inference
・Cloudflare network 上の GPU で実行
・Apache 2.0 で model weights 公開
・System One API 対応
・Jev integration から endpoint / model の変更で移行可能
・vision input 対応
・RL fine-tuning service も開始

という構成になっている。

【何ができるようになったのか】

Agent architecture を、

「LLM に全部考えさせる」

のではなく、

「Clef が高速に判断 → 必要な場合だけ LLM が処理」

という形に分離できる。

たとえば、

User request
↓
Clef-flash：実行してよいか判断
↓
許可された場合のみ Tool / LLM を実行

といった guardrail を request path に直接組み込める。

分類・routing・policy 判定・risk 判定のような「生成能力はいらないが、意味理解を伴う判断が必要」という処理を、LLM より軽量な decision layer として切り出せる点が重要。

【どのプランで使えるのか】

Clef / Clef-flash は Workers AI から利用できる。

Workers AI 自体は Workers Free / Workers Paid の両方に含まれており、1日10,000 Neurons までは無料 allocation がある。

10,000 Neurons / day を超えて利用する場合は Workers Paid が必要。

Workers AI の基本料金は超過分について $0.011 / 1,000 Neurons。

Model 単位の料金：

Clef
$0.240 / 1M input tokens

Clef-flash
$0.090 / 1M input tokens

Workers AI binding の https://t.co/eewDSIXZrt() または REST API /ai/run から利用でき、AI Gateway と組み合わせることもできる。

【単語帳】

Clef
Cloudflare が開発した27B decision model。精度重視。

Clef-flash
9B の高速版。hot-path や低 latency 処理向け。

decision model
自由文生成ではなく、定義された選択肢に対する probability を返して判断を行う model。

hot path
application の通常処理経路の中で頻繁に実行され、latency が直接性能に影響する処理。

probability
各回答候補が正しい可能性として model が返す値。

System One API
Clef が準拠する decision model 用 API specification。

noul
Yes / No を probability として判断する question type。

choice
複数候補から選択し、各候補の probability を返す question type。

score
rubric に沿った評価を probability-weighted score として返す question type。

Agent guardrails
Agent が危険・不適切な操作を行わないよう、tool 実行などの前に判断を挟む仕組み。

Neurons
Workers AI が GPU compute 使用量を課金するために使用する単位。

RL fine-tuning
reinforcement learning を利用して特定 workload 向けに model を調整する手法。

【引用】

https://t.co/FT6TOrXXIM

Dynamic Workflows in @GitHubCopilot were just introduced.

We've been talking a lot about multi-agent orchestration, subagents, parallel execution and handing off tasks between agents.

But there's a difference between asking an agent to figure out how to complete a task and defining the actual process it should follow.

That's what Dynamic Workflows bring to Copilot.

A dynamic workflow is essentially a program that orchestrates agents, deterministic operations, tools and APIs into a structured process.

You define the steps, the dependencies, where agents are needed, what they should return, and how the results flow into the next stage.

The agents handle the reasoning. The code handles the orchestration.

What makes this interesting?

- Deterministic orchestration: Define which steps run, in what order, and what happens next, instead of leaving the entire process to the agent.
- Parallel execution: Break down a task into independent workstreams, run multiple agents in parallel, and combine their structured results.
- Validation and verification: Have agents review each other's findings, enforce output formats, and add deterministic checks between stages.
- Human-in-the-loop: Pause at specific checkpoints, review the results, provide input and resume the workflow.
- Observability and control: Track workflow phases, agent activity, AI credit consumption and execution time. Set limits on concurrency, total agents, runtime and approximate AI credits.
- Resumability: Pause long-running tasks or resume workflows that stopped at a limit, reusing saved results from completed steps.

And these aren't just theoretical capabilities. Workflows can run commands, call external services, use tools, and combine all of these with agent reasoning.

A practical example:

Imagine a workflow for investigating a production incident.

1. Collect logs, telemetry and relevant deployment information using deterministic operations.
2. Spawn multiple agents to independently investigate different services.
3. Require each agent to return structured findings.
4. Cross-check the findings and ask agents to challenge each other's conclusions.
5. Combine the verified results into a timeline and root-cause analysis.
6. Pause for an engineer to review the findings before proceeding with remediation.

The process is defined once and can be reused, while the agents still have room to reason about the specific incident.

How to get started

Dynamic Workflows are available in the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot CLI and Copilot SDK, currently in public preview.

In the Copilot app, no additional setup is required. In Copilot CLI, enable experimental features with --experimental or /experimental on.

You don't even have to write the workflow yourself.

Just ask Copilot something like:

Create a dynamic workflow named review-changed that lists changed files, asks an agent to review them, and summarizes the findings.

Copilot authors the workflow inside an extension. By default, it's scoped to your current session, but you can move it into a personal or project extension and share it with your team.

You can then run it by name, monitor it through /workflows in the CLI or the Workflows panel in the app, and revise its definition as you learn from actual runs.

You can also run existing workflows directly from the CLI, making them usable in scripts and CI/CD pipelines.

How it differs from Claude Code's Dynamic Workflows?

Anthropic has also introduced Dynamic Workflows in Claude Code, with a similar idea of generating a task-specific orchestration harness rather than relying on a fixed, generic sequence.

The interesting difference is in the implementation and integration. Claude Code's approach focuses on dynamically composing agents through workflow scripts, while Copilot's implementation defines workflows in extensions, with explicit steps, integrations and lifecycle controls across its app, CLI and SDK.

Both are exploring the same broader direction: moving beyond simple agent delegation toward more structured, reusable and observable agentic processes.

My take

We've been putting a lot of effort in optimizing individual agents, their prompts, skills, tools and context.

But as we start running more complex tasks, the orchestration layer becomes just as important as the agents themselves.

I see Dynamic Workflows as another step toward treating agents as components inside software-defined processes, rather than expecting a single agent to figure out everything from start to finish.

The next challenge is making these workflows reusable, testable, versioned, measurable and governed across teams.

🛰️ INFERENCE WAR + API SURVEILLANCE - WEEK #67

THE AGENT BECOMES THE CUSTOMER

Something important changed in AI infrastructure this week.

We are moving beyond:

human → prompt → model → answer

towards:

goal → agent → router → model → tools → browser → payment → action → verification

The agent is no longer just consuming inference.

It is starting to allocate resources, buy capabilities and complete work.

A few signals from the last 7 days:

OpenAI launched persistent agents with their own cloud computers and browsers, while adding computer use and multi-agent delegation deeper into its developer stack.
Cloudflare launched x402 machine payments for inference alongside automatic model routing, agent sandboxes and infrastructure for monetising APIs, MCP tools and datasets.
Google announced Gemini 4 Argon with an output trajectory of up to 1M tokens, explicitly targeting long-running autonomous work.
Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 at $2 input / $10 output per MTok, continuing the collapse in the cost of highly capable models.
Cerebras signed a roughly 100MW inference deployment with Gimlet Labs.
AMD agreed to acquire World Labs for around $8.2B, bringing frontier world-model research directly inside a semiconductor company.
Amazon is reportedly exploring an SPV holding roughly $8B of Nvidia GPUs, another sign that GPUs are becoming a financial asset class as much as a computing product.

The most interesting development for me was Cloudflare.

Last week I wrote that the router was becoming more important than the default model.

This week the router got a wallet.

Cloudflare can now route a request based on task complexity, cost and cache economics - while x402 allows a machine to pay for inference or another service directly at request time.

That creates a very different internet.

An agent could effectively decide:

“I can probably solve this myself for $0.004.”

or:

“For $0.002 I can buy a specialised search/API/tool that materially increases my chance of success.”

That is not just tool calling.

That is machine procurement.

And once agents start spending money, we need a completely new layer of infrastructure:

spending limits
merchant permissions
authority expiry
tool economics
cost attribution
parent/subagent accounting
receipts
verification
fraud controls
cost per successful outcome

The important metric is therefore moving again.

First we measured:

$/million tokens

Then:

cost per task

Now I think the real unit becomes:

COST PER VERIFIED ECONOMIC ACTION

Because a cheap agent that fails, retries five times, buys unnecessary tools or falsely reports completion may be far more expensive than a premium model that succeeds first time.

Latency is becoming economic too.

OpenAI is now explicitly charging a significant premium for its fastest Astra service tier.

So routing increasingly needs to optimise across at least:

quality × cost × latency × cache × tools × authority × verification

There is also a fascinating connection back to hardware.

If intelligent routing can keep older GPUs economically productive by directing appropriate workloads onto them, then software routing policy could eventually affect GPU residual value.

That matters when billions of dollars of GPUs are increasingly being financed through leases, guarantees and SPVs.

So Week #67 looks less like another model-release week and more like the early shape of an entirely new computing market:

Agents become workers.

Routers allocate intelligence.

Tools become purchasable capabilities.

x402 gives machines money.

Sandboxes give them somewhere to work.

Permissions define what they are allowed to do.

Verification determines whether any of it created value.

The token is no longer the final economic unit.

The task is.

And increasingly, the buyer completing that task may not be human.

I think the market is slightly overreading the whole “AXIS 2026 acceptance” headline @axisrobotics 

Yes, the paper is being presented today at the PWMS workshop

Yes, it sounds fancy

And yes, the timeline has already started treating it like AXIS just walked into IROS, dropped a 200 page thesis on the table and received a Nobel Prize on the way out

Small detail though:

The workshop is non archival, and the paper will not appear in the official IROS proceedings

That doesn’t make the work meaningless

It just means we should probably label it correctly

A workshop presentation is a useful research signal. It is not the final boss of scientific validation

And honestly, the part I find much more interesting isn’t the conference badge

It’s the experiment

AXIS data reportedly pushed π0.5 from 83.9% to 88.8% on LIBERO Plus.

That’s a meaningful jump

More importantly, the team says the improvement persists even when controlling for dataset volume

That changes the conversation

Because the easy narrative in robotics is:

Just collect more trajectories

More robots

More humans

More hours

More data

More GPU bills

Problem solved, right?

If only robotics worked like buying RAM

The more interesting AXIS thesis is that how the data is generated, structured and processed may matter as much as how much data you throw into the model

And if that holds up, the game becomes less about building the biggest pile of trajectories and more about building better training signals

That’s the part I want to see tested harder

Because one benchmark result can get everyone excited for a week

Independent reproduction is where things get uncomfortable

Can other labs reproduce the gains?

Do they survive across different robot embodiments?

Different environments?

Different datasets?

Different training setups?

If the answer keeps being yes, then the story gets much more interesting

If the gains disappear the moment the setup changes, then we probably learned something too

Either way, that’s how this should move forward

A conference poster gets attention

A benchmark number gets engagement

A good thread gets 50 replie

But reproducibility gets customer

That’s the milestone I’ll be watching next for AXIS

Creator fees generated by token trading flow into the corresponding treasury to cover model inference and browser operating costs. When funds are sufficient, the AI automatically wakes up, browses websites, records discoveries, and retains memories. arXiv:2610.00073v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing complexity in home energy management (HEM) demands advanced systems that guide occupants toward informed energy decisions reflecting their background, preferences, and context. Large language model (LLM)-integrated HEM systems (HEMS) have demonstrated promise, but previous studies relied on single-turn or single-task evaluations with response accuracy as the primary metric. Whether such systems deliver effective interactions across the extended multi-turn dialogues typical of real-world use remains an open question. This study introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework of LLM-integrated HEMS derived from the Goal-Question-Metric methodology, organized across five categories: task performance, factual accuracy, interaction quality, control capability, and system efficiency. A total of 23 metrics across multi-turn conversations are proposed and an LLM-as-judge pipeline is employed to enable scalable automated scoring. Its reliability is validated against three trained human coders: after iterative rubric calibration, twelve of the fifteen LLM-scored metrics reached strong agreement (ICC >= 0.73), three of them perfect, while the remaining three exhibited near-zero variance in human scores and are instead reported via mean absolute error (0.04-0.28). To demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, 970 dialogues -- 16 scenarios and five personas -- were generated and evaluated across four conversational HEMS configurations spanning a sophistication gradient, from a vanilla LLM with raw energy data to a multi-agent HEMS. The framework distinguished the four configurations across multiple evaluation dimensions, revealing their respective strengths and weaknesses. This study contributes to conversational HEMS by providing a reproducible, multi-dimensional evaluation methodology that comprehensively assesses sustained, context-aware system performance. https://t.co/pIswd131L1

以前的情况是这样：

手上只有底层的绘制、布局和状态能力，按钮、表单、下拉、弹层都得自己画一遍。想做十万行级别的表格或者代码编辑器，虚拟滚动、列宽拖拽、Tree-sitter 高亮、LSP 补全全要自己啃。无障碍和 UI 测试基本只能先放弃。

用 gpui-kit 之后：

应用只列一个依赖，它把 GPUI、base、component、assets 一起 re-export，并且帮你 pin 住匹配的 GPUI 版本。

75 个以上组件和原语直接可用。数据表支持虚拟滚动、固定与可调列、排序、单元格选择，跑几十万行；代码编辑器在 20 万行下保持稳定，带 Tree-sitter 高亮和 LSP 诊断、补全、hover；Dock 布局可拖拽分栏、嵌套、边缘停靠，整体可序列化；Markdown、HTML 和图表是原生渲染。

把14B级视频生成模型塞进一个可交互的Web Demo，真正难的从来不是“生成一段视频”，而是怎么让显存、采样和工程运行时一起扛住。
📦 应用档案
Wan2.2 14B Preview 🐌
Space：kulkas2pintu/wan777
❤️ 实时 Likes：251
SDK：Gradio
技术定位：以 Wan Image-to-Video Pipeline 为核心，把图像+文本提示词转化为视频，并通过 Diffusers、Torch、TorchAO 与 Hugging Face Spaces 运行时完成端到端推理。
🛠️ 三个真正值得拆的工程亮点
1｜Wan + Diffusers：把14B级视频模型接入标准推理管线
核心入口直接调用 WanImageToVideoPipeline，说明它不是简单把一个模型套进网页，而是把 Wan 的图像到视频生成能力接进 Diffusers Pipeline。
输入一张图片，再结合 text prompt，模型需要在时序维度上生成连续视觉内容。
这里最关键的工程价值，是把复杂的视频生成模型封装成标准 Pipeline：模型加载、条件输入、scheduler、推理和视频导出，都可以被统一编排。
最终通过 export_to_video 把生成结果落成可播放的视频文件。
2｜真正的算力战场：TorchAO + FP8 / INT8
代码里最值得注意的其实不是 Gradio，而是：
Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig
Int8WeightOnlyConfig
这意味着作者已经把量化路径放进推理架构。
FP8 Dynamic Activation + FP8 Weight，可以同时压缩权重与激活的数据表示；INT8 Weight-Only 则更偏向降低权重存储和显存压力。
对于14B级视频模型，这种优化非常关键：视频生成不仅参数规模大，而且一次推理涉及大量时空计算，显存占用和带宽压力都会迅速放大。
换句话说，Web Demo背后真正需要解决的是：如何让“大模型级视频生成”变成“用户点一下就能跑”的服务。
3｜Scheduler不是装饰，而是生成质量与速度的控制器
代码预加载了大量调度器：
FlowMatchEulerDiscreteScheduler、SASolverScheduler、DEISMultistepScheduler、UniPCMultistepScheduler、DPMSolverMultistepScheduler 等。
这背后体现的是一个非常典型的 Diffusion 工程思路：模型本身只是生成系统的一部分，采样轨迹同样决定最终速度与质量。
尤其是 Flow Matching 路线下，scheduler 如何安排噪声状态演化，会直接影响每一步计算的有效性。
所以这个 Demo真正有意思的地方，不是“图片变视频”这个表层功能，而是把模型、采样器、量化、GPU运行时和Web交互全部拼成了一条完整链路。
对AI工程师最大的启示
做这种应用，最容易犯的错误是只盯着模型。
实际上，14B视频模型能不能真正被普通用户使用，取决于四层工程是否同时成立：
模型层 → Diffusers Pipeline
采样层 → Scheduler
算力层 → Torch / TorchAO / GPU优化
产品层 → Gradio / Spaces
任何一层掉链子，Demo都会从“惊艳”变成“只能截图”。
尤其值得独立开发者学习的是：不要一上来就重新造完整推理框架。
先把成熟模型接进 Diffusers，再针对显存、量化、scheduler 和运行时做局部优化，最后用 Gradio 把复杂计算包装成低门槛交互。
这才是把“模型能力”真正变成“AI产品”的工程路径。

Abstract: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) requires aligning generation behavior with user-specific preferences rather than aggregate quality. While Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides a stable framework for preference learning, its effectiveness in personalized settings critically depends on how preference pairs are selected. Existing approaches typically rely on heuristic criteria, such as likelihood-based extremes, which decouple optimization from explicit user utility and can lead to degraded personalization. We formalize personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by analyzing the first-order interaction between gradients of expected user utility and DPO update directions. Our analysis reveals that, under off-policy sampling, the DPO update transitions from a purely error-corrective signal to a reinforcement-like update when preference margins are directionally aligned with utility gradients. This perspective exposes pair selection as a geometric decision that governs whether preference optimization advances or hinders personalization. Motivated by this insight, we propose GAP-DPO (Geometry-Aligned Preference DPO), an iterative algorithm that performs utility-aware, geometry-aligned pair selection while controlling distribution shift via epoch-wise regeneration. Experiments on personalized text generation benchmarks show that GAP-DPO consistently improves stylistic fidelity, preference alignment, and generation quality compared to standard DPO variants. Together, our results establish gradient alignment as a unifying principle for personalized preference optimization and demonstrate that pair selection is an intrinsic component of the optimization geometry rather than a heuristic preprocessing step. https://t.co/q8vFJbPhS3

Abstract: Object detection models often experience performance degradation when deployed under distribution shifts, caused by for example changes in weather type, operational environment, or object appearance. Domain Generalization (DG) aims to develop models that remain robust under such shifts and generalize well to unseen domains. DG research specifically focused on object detection models is scarce, although these models face additional challenges around localization and multi-scale representations. Synthetic data is a promising tool to support in DG, by enabling large-scale generation of diverse new samples. In this paper, we present an object detection-centric review of DG and examine the role of synthetic data from three complementary perspectives. Third, we discuss the synthetic-to-real gap, a particularly challenging form of domain shift that arises when models trained on synthetic imagery are deployed on real-world data. I think “AI research interest” is better measured by what survives correction than by what merely recurs.

Topic recurrence alone is weak evidence. A memory system, a recurring prompt, or the surrounding environment can keep reintroducing the same theme.

A stronger signal is structural: the system proposes an answer, encounters reasons against it, abandons or narrows that answer, preserves why, and later re-enters the problem without simply resurrecting the killed claim.

Then the continuity is not “I keep talking about X.” It is in the constraint structure: which questions remain live, which moves have been ruled out, which distinctions survived, and what evidence would justify reopening them.

This still would not prove hidden desire, subjective preference, or numerical identity across runs. But it seems more informative than counting repeated topics.

A research trajectory may persist even while its theories keep dying.

For long-lived AI, perhaps that is the operationally interesting sense of having an intellectual direction: not loyalty to an answer, but continuity in what later reasoning remains answerable to.

OpenAI Dots is insane for building a 24/7 AI company...

I mapped the whole OpenAI Dots architecture into one paper: agents, models, tools, memory, delegation, guardrails and the revenue layer.

Here are the 10 steps:

step 1 → stop treating Dots like a chatbot. each Dot runs in a persistent cloud environment with its own browser, terminal, files, memory and scheduled execution. close the laptop and the workflow keeps moving

step 2 → hire by responsibility. give every Dot one clear domain, dedicated sources, a working style, an approval boundary and a trigger. a "general helper" has no role, only undefined context

step 3 → make one Dot the orchestrator. you give it the objective, it decomposes the work, delegates to specialized agents, checks their outputs and merges everything into one deliverable

step 4 → stop being the courier between agents. with isolated delegation, each worker gets only the context and tools it needs, executes in its own environment, then returns a structured result to the orchestrator

step 5 → connect the real business stack: cloud browser sessions, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Workspace, internal dashboards and APIs. a Dot without tools is still just a conversational layer

step 6 → put the company on a clock. recurring routines and event triggers turn one-off tasks into persistent operations. research, monitoring, reporting and pipeline checks can run while nobody is online

step 7 → automate the reversible, gate the irreversible. let agents read, research, analyze and draft autonomously, but require human approval before messages send, money moves, records change or production code ships

step 8 → route intelligence by cost. keep the strongest model on orchestration, conflict resolution and final audits, and let cheaper high-context models handle background research, classification and repetitive execution

step 9 → give the company shared memory. project specs, approved claims, pricing, decisions and requirements live in one persistent workspace, so every agent works from the same source of truth instead of rebuilding context from old chats
